extracted.intended_audience: PinkNews readers; general public interested in LGBTQ+ issues and social media moderation
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting on the application and enforcement of Twitter's hateful conduct policy, specifically around misgendering/deadnaming of trans people and the platform's moderation responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misgendering and deadnaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter’s hateful conduct policy prohibits users from misgendering trans people or deliberately deadnaming them as it 'dehumanising [and] degrades' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted rationale from the policy: misgendering/deadnaming is considered dehumanising and degrading. The article uses this policy language to explain why the Babylon Bee and others were blocked for tweets mocking Rachel Levine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement actions: removal, read-only periods, and suspension for primary hateful use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under its rules, users can be ordered to remove an offending tweet and 'serve a period of time in read-only mode before they can tweet again'. An account can be suspended if moderators find the account’s 'primary use' is 'engaging in hateful conduct as defined in this policy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences described in the article: Twitter warned The Babylon Bee it had broken rules against 'hateful conduct' and would be blocked from tweeting until the 'violative tweet' is removed; the offending tweet was later removed (unclear whether by the user or moderators); other accounts (Not The Bee, Christian Post) were blocked, and individuals (Kyle Mann) locked out for offensive tweets. These enforcement mechanisms (content removal, temporary read-only, suspension for repeated/primary hateful use) are the policy's stated remedies.
